title: Bandits with Single-Peaked Preferences and Limited Resources
claim: A structure that looks irregular under one ordering becomes simple and unimodal once the items are reordered.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, left-to-right, same curves with reordered x-axis
description: Two side-by-side line plots share the same axes: arm index on the x-axis and reward from 0 to 1 on the y-axis. Each plot shows three smooth curves with markers, labelled u1 (green squares), u2 (blue circles) and u3 (red triangles). In panel (a), labelled 'An SP instance', arms are ordered 1 to 5 and the curves zigzag, with several local peaks and dips. In panel (b), labelled 'A PSP instance', the same values are reordered as 1, 2, 5, 4, 3. Every curve is now unimodal, with one peak and then a decline. The eye goes to the red peak at arm 5 in the right panel, which makes the contrast between jagged and smooth curves clear.
caption: Illustration of PSP and SP instances. Each subfigure consists of curves representing the expected rewards of user-arm pairs. The instance in [ref] is SP, since if we reorder the arms, we get the PSP instance in [ref] .
abstract: We study an online stochastic matching problem in which an algorithm sequentially matches $U$ users to $K$ arms, aiming to maximize cumulative reward over $T$ rounds under budget constraints. Without structural assumptions, computing the optimal matching is NP-hard, making online learning computationally infeasible. To overcome this barrier, we focus on single-peaked preferences -- a well-established structure in social choice theory, where users' preferences are unimodal with respect to a common order over arms. We devise an efficient algorithm for the offline budgeted matching problem, and leverage it into an efficient online algorithm with a regret of $\tilde O(UKT^{2/3})$. Our approach relies on a novel PQ tree-based order approximation method. If the single-peaked structure is known, we develop an efficient UCB-like algorithm that achieves a regret bound of $\tilde O(U\sqrt{TK})$.
